9.42: When you are offended by any man's shameless behaviour, immediately ask yourself: Is it possible, then, that there should be no shameless men in the world? It is not possible. Do not, then, demand what is impossible. For this man too is one of those shameless men who must necessarily be in the world. Let the same thoughts be present to your mind in the case of the rogue, and the faithless man, and every man who does wrong in any way. For as soon as you remind yourself that it is impossible that such men should not exist, you will become more kindly disposed towards each one individually. It is useful to see this too, as soon as the occasion arises: what virtue nature has given to man to set against every wrongful act. For she has given to man, as an antidote against the stupid man, gentleness, and against another kind of man some other power. And in every case it is possible for you to correct, by teaching, the man who has gone astray; for every man who errs misses his aim and has gone astray. Besides, how have you been harmed? For you will find that none of those you are irritated with has done anything by which your mind could be made worse; and that which is evil and harmful to you has its foundation only in the mind. And what harm is done, or what is strange, if a man who has not been taught does the acts of an untaught man? Consider whether you should not rather blame yourself, because you did not expect such a man to err in such a way. For your reason gave you the means to suppose that he was likely to make this mistake, and yet you have forgotten, and are amazed that he has erred. But most of all, when you blame a man as faithless or ungrateful, turn to yourself. For the fault is clearly your own, whether you trusted that a man with such a disposition would keep his promise, or, when doing a kindness, you did not do it freely, nor in such a way as to have received all the benefit from the act itself. For what more do you want when you have done a man a service? Are you not content that you have done something in keeping with your nature, and do you want to be paid for it? It is as if the eye demanded a reward for seeing, or the feet for walking. For just as these parts of the body are formed for a particular purpose, and by working according to their own makeup obtain what is their own, so too man is formed by nature for acts of kindness; and when he has done anything kind, or in any other way helpful to the common good, he has acted in keeping with his makeup, and he gets what is his own.
